label: CBSE 12 Maths 2025 65/1/3 Probability MCQ
reason: flawed: CBSE 2025 65/1/3 prints P(M and N) = 0.5 > P(N) = 0.2; scheme key A
solution:
**Note:** As printed, these numbers cannot all be true: \(P(M \cap N) = 0.5\) is larger than \(P(N) = 0.2\). The working below follows the question as set, which gives CBSE's key (A).

Both events in the required conditional probability are complements, so use De Morgan first: \(M' \cap N' = \overline{M \cup N}\). Now \(P(M \cup N) = P(M) + P(N) - P(M \cap N) = 0.6 + 0.2 - 0.5 = 0.3\), so \(P(M' \cap N') = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7\), and \(P(N') = 1 - 0.2 = 0.8\). Therefore \(P(M'/N') = \frac{P(M' \cap N')}{P(N')} = \frac{0.7}{0.8} = \frac{7}{8}\), which is option (A) \(\frac{7}{8}\). A closing note for the careful reader: the data as printed cannot describe any real pair of events, because \(P(M \cap N) = 0.5\) exceeds \(P(N) = 0.2\) and an intersection can never be more likely than either event containing it. The computation above is nevertheless the one the question intends, and it is what the official key records.

label: CBSE 12 Maths 2022 65/5/1 Probability (written)
reason: flawed: CBSE 2022 65/5/1 prints data forcing P(A and B) = 3/4 > P(A) = 1/2
solution:
**Note:** As printed, these numbers cannot all be true: they make \(P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{3}{4}\), larger than \(P(A) = \dfrac{1}{2}\). The working below follows the question as set.

The third datum is about a union of complements, so convert it with De Morgan's law: \(\overline{A} \cup \overline{B} = \overline{A \cap B}\), hence \(P\left(\overline{A} \cup \overline{B}\right) = 1 - P(A \cap B)\).

Therefore \(1 - P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{4}\), giving \(P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{3}{4}\).

A and B are independent precisely when \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)\). Here \(P(A)\,P(B) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{7}{12} = \dfrac{7}{24}\), and \(\dfrac{3}{4} \neq \dfrac{7}{24}\). So the events A and B are not independent.

Note: the three figures quoted in the question are not mutually consistent as probabilities. They force \(P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{3}{4}\), which is impossible because an intersection can never be more likely than either event on its own, and \(P(A) = \dfrac{1}{2}\). That is a flaw in the data as set, not in the working above; on the comparison the question actually asks for, the verdict is the same either way.

label: CBSE 12 Chemistry 2023 56/1/2 Chemical Kinetics MCQ
reason: flawed: CBSE 2023 56/1/2: k = 0.693/30 = 2.31e-2 per min, no option prints it; the scheme gives full marks for any option
solution:
**Note:** No option is correct as printed. A half life of 30 minutes gives \(k = 2{\cdot}31 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\), and every option is at least ten times smaller. CBSE's marking scheme gave full marks for any option.

For a FIRST ORDER reaction the half-life is related to the rate constant by
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{k}\)

"50% completion in 30 minutes" IS the half-life, so
\(k = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{30} = 0{\cdot}0231\ \mathrm{min^{-1}} = 2{\cdot}31 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

[NONE of the four options carries this value. The nearest, \(2{\cdot}31 \times 10^{-3}\), has the right digits but is a factor of ten too small, as are all four, which sit between \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-3}\) where the answer is of order \(10^{-2}\). The marking scheme records the defect and instructs examiners to award full marks FOR ANY OPTION. Work the arithmetic, not the options.]

The unit is a check on the working: a first order constant must come out as reciprocal time, and reciprocal minutes is what dividing a pure number by 30 minutes gives.

label: CBSE 12 Maths 2023 65/4/2 Differential Equations MCQ
reason: key: CBSE 2023 65/4/2 marking scheme keys B (one); every curve y + 1 = C(x - 1) passes through (1, -1), never (1, 2), so the count is zero = A. Key corrected with a notice (owner policy 2026-10-29).
solution:
**Note:** CBSE's marking scheme keys (B) one. Every curve of the family \( y + 1 = C(x - 1) \) passes through \( (1, -1) \), so none can pass through \( (1, 2) \): the number of solutions is zero, option (A), which is the answer shown here.

Away from \( x = 1 \) and \( y = -1 \) the equation separates as \( \dfrac{dy}{y + 1} = \dfrac{dx}{x - 1} \); integrating gives \( \log|y + 1| = \log|x - 1| + \log|C| \), that is \( y + 1 = C(x - 1) \). Imposing \( y(1) = 2 \) requires \( 3 = C \times 0 = 0 \), which is false for every C, and the constant solution \( y = -1 \) lost when we divided does not pass through \( (1, 2) \) either. The obstruction is visible in the equation itself: at \( x = 1,\ y = 2 \) the right hand side reads \( \dfrac{3}{0} \), so no derivative can be assigned there. Hence no differentiable function satisfies both the equation and \( y(1) = 2 \), and the number of solutions is zero. The only curve through \( (1, 2) \) satisfying the equation in its differential form \( (x - 1)\,dy = (y + 1)\,dx \) is the vertical line \( x = 1 \), which is not a function of x; counting that degenerate curve is the one reading under which CBSE's count of one arises.

label: CBSE 12 Chemistry 2024 56/3/1 Chemical Kinetics MCQ
reason: key: CBSE 2024 56/3/1 marking scheme keys A (remains constant); a catalyst lowers Ea, so by Arrhenius k increases = C. Key corrected with a notice (owner policy 2026-10-29).
solution:
**Note:** CBSE's marking scheme keys (A) remains constant. A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so the rate constant increases, option (C), which is the answer shown here.

The RATE CONSTANT INCREASES.

A catalyst works by offering the reaction an ALTERNATIVE PATH with a LOWER ACTIVATION ENERGY. By the Arrhenius equation
\(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\)
a smaller \(E_a\) makes the exponential term larger, so \(k\) itself is larger.

That is in fact the only way the rate CAN rise here. Adding a catalyst changes none of the concentrations, so in \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^m[\mathrm{B}]^n\) the concentration factors are exactly what they were. If the rate has gone up, the constant must have gone up with it.

What a catalyst does NOT change is the position of equilibrium. It leaves \(\Delta H\), \(\Delta S\) and \(\Delta G\) untouched, and it lowers the barrier in both directions equally, so the equilibrium constant is unchanged: the reaction simply reaches the same equilibrium sooner.
